title: Firouzja, Giri Lead Total Chess Semifinals; Carlsen Forfeits Final Game
summary:
GM Alireza Firouzja started with a 4-0 blitz victory against GM Fabiano Caruana, lost that lead in a single rapid game, but ultimately won the day 12-8 as the grueling Semifinals of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 began. The other clash in the top bracket went the way of GM Anish Giri, who won the fast-classic game against GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave to complete a 14.5-5.5 victory. Caruana and Vachier-Lagrave will have a chance to hit back on Wednesday for a spot in the Final.

GM Magnus Carlsen got off to a near-perfect start as he scored 11.5/12 against GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, becoming the only player to wrap up victory before the final game. Their matchup ended in controversy, however, since Carlsen declined to appear for that game—where his 2800 status and world number-one spot would be on the line—leaving Assaubayeva sitting at the board until she was awarded a forfeit win to make the score 11.5-8.5.

Day eight, the second of the Semifinals, starts on Wednesday, November 18, at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Knockout 1: Giri, Firouzja Lead Battle To Win Tournament

Knockout 2: Niemann, Nepomniachtchi Lead On 'Tilted Tuesday'

Knockout 3: Martirosyan Comes Back Vs. Rapport, Arjun Leads From Blitz

Knockout 4: Mamedyarov, So Lead

Knockout 5: Carlsen Wins Then Forfeits; Artemiev Dominates Vs. Hong

Knockout 6: Praggnanandhaa, Mishra Lead After Shortest/Longest Matches

If the players felt two games of fast-classic chess a day was tough, most felt the knockout format was even tougher, with seven games and another seven-hour day. When asked about goals, GM Levon Aronian mentioned "at this moment surviving is important," GM Jorden van Foreest commented, "my head is just aching, just too much chess today," while Giri reflected, "FIDE maybe needs a commission to take care of players—the Players Wellbeing Commission."

Jorden van Foreest had a tough day. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

The format was also unusual, with the day starting with blitz before the time control got progressively longer. GM Hikaru Nakamura described that as "ridiculous," explaining how chess events usually start with the longer formats first. The scoring was also original, with GMs Ian Nepomniachtchi and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov among the players to note it was puzzling that rapid games were worth four times as much as blitz, not double as we're used to from events such as the Grand Chess Tour.

The format is four blitz games (1 point a win), then two rapid games (4 points), then a single fast-classic game (8 points) each day. The margin of victory is largely unimportant, since if the losing player wins the next day the match winner will be decided in armageddon, though there the player with the most points overall does get to choose the color.

You can watch Nakamura's recap of the day's action below:

Knockout 1: Giri, Firouzja Lead Battle To Win Tournament

Although all 24 players are still in action, the one bracket that really matters is the first, where tournament victory and the top-four prizes are on the line. It was expected to be tight, which made it shocking when Firouzja raced to a 4-0 victory in the blitz over Caruana.

"The blitz was really awful, I was just blundering everything every game," said Caruana, who got some fleeting chances of his own.

Caruana could have won the second game on the spot with 34.Rg1!, threatening mate on g7 and winning the black queen, but he took on b4 instead.

Firouzja's fantastic start was wiped out in the first rapid game, however, as Caruana smoothly converted a win with the black pieces.

Alireza Firouzja walks around the playing hall. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

It then seemed as though Caruana was going to take the lead as he built up a close-to-winning position with the white pieces, but Firouzja is one of the most resourceful players in chess, and he turned things around with a dramatic attack. That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao analyzes below.

That meant Firouzja took a four-point lead into the classical game—with Caruana needing to win on demand. Of the nine players in that situation, only two managed, and only one with the black pieces.

Firouzja vs. Caruana could have gone either way. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Caruana did well out of the opening, with Firouzja admitting the game "got out of hand, out of my control," but he found a narrow path to safety and then was even winning before taking a draw that clinched the day's match 12-8.

The winner of that matchup will play either Giri or Vachier-Lagrave in the Final, with Giri emerging on top after the first day. What was perhaps surprising was that he took the lead in the blitz, though as he noted: "On a good day I can play well! I’m much less stable than Maxime, but I have days when I play like a world-class blitz player."

I'm much less stable than Maxime, but I have days when I play like a world-class blitz player.

—Anish Giri

Anish Giri got the better of Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in blitz. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Three blitz games were drawn, with two missed wins for Giri, but he did win the remaining game when Vachier-Lagrave grabbed a pawn.

The rapid games were both drawn, with Vachier-Lagrave pointing out that Giri wasn't too focused on taking his winning chances in the second since a one-point lead or a five-point lead would make no difference to the match situation. Vachier-Lagrave in either case knew he had to win on demand with the black pieces to turn things around.

Maxime Vachier-Lagrave has enjoyed the tournament, but suffered a tough day. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

The Frenchman came to the confessional after the opening to note that he preferred the position Caruana had achieved in a similar situation. Vachier-Lagrave got little, and said he "over-pushed." Giri was able to take over, as his "hanging pawns" went from a weakness to a huge strength.

That win took Giri up to world number-eight, but Vachier-Lagrave has a chance to hit back. What lessons from the day will he take into Wednesday? "Hopefully I don’t remember anything I’ve done from today!"

Hopefully I don't remember anything I've done from today!

—Maxime Vachier-Lagrave

Knockout 2: Niemann, Nepomniachtchi Lead On 'Tilted Tuesday'

The best description of one of the battles for fifth place came from Nepomniachtchi, who commented: "Today’s Tuesday. It was a little bit of tilt, first for me after the first blitz game, and then for Jan-Krzysztof. We missed Titled Tuesday, but Tilted Tuesday is all down here!"

We missed Titled Tuesday, but Tilted Tuesday is all down here!

—Ian Nepomniachtchi

Duda was shocked at his good fortune in the first game. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

That saga began with GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda winning the first blitz game in a queen endgame with two pawns apiece.

Duda won another two blitz games for a 3-1 scoreline, but then in the second rapid game Duda lost an exchange-up position. The Polish number-one suddenly found himself needing to win the classical game on demand, but he only fell to defeat in what should have been a holdable position.

Things ultimately went Ian Nepomniachtchi's way. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

In the other match, GM Liem Le started with a sparkling blitz win and took a 2.5-1.5 lead, with GM Hans Niemann later saying that the stress of having to come back from that was "borderline unhealthy." Both rapid games were drawn, so that Niemann had to win on demand in fast classic—which is just what he did. "I’m coming in clutch when needed!" he said, after Le stumbled into a lost position at the very end.

Hans Niemann overcame Liem Le. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Knockout 3: Martirosyan Comes Back Vs. Rapport, Arjun Leads From Blitz

By the third knockout, players are only playing for ninth place, with GM Arjun Erigaisi commenting, "I don't think it's super important!" The Indian star took a 3.5-0.5 lead over Van Foreest in the blitz, then the players exchanged wins in rapid. It came down to a must-win game for Black in the classical chess, but instead we got a fast and contentless 30-move draw.

Arjun defeated Jorden van Foreest. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Arjun explained: "Classical first would have been a nicer order. This way it came down to classical and I had White, and I tried to play safe." Why didn't Van Foreest try to rock the board? He said he might have done if he was incentivized by a battle for first place, but as it was: "Honestly I’m pretty happy with the draw. It sounds weird, but first of all my head is just aching, just too much chess today, and let’s be real, we’re not really playing for anything major. In general a draw against Arjun is good."

Let's be real, we're not really playing for anything major.

—Jorden van Foreest

The other match in the bracket at least featured one of the day's most memorable moments. GM Richard Rapport, who won the blitz 3-1, also won the rapid after pulling off a great escape with the help of a desperado rook.

Richard Rapport pulled off mate-in-1 from a lost position vs. Praggnanandhaa, but this swindle vs. Martirosyan is just as good! https://t.co/YjBoTOrbtV #TotalChess https://t.co/JNawjz0GPL

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 17, 2026

That was a swindle comparable to landing mate-in-one against GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu from a lost position earlier in the tournament, but karma came back to bite in the next game.

Martirosyan recovered fast! Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

In fact, the miss by GM Haik Martirosyan had made no real difference at all, since in either case he would have to win on demand with the black pieces in the classical game. That's just what he did, with Rapport's position collapsing until he resigned on move 26.

Knockout 4: Mamedyarov, So Lead

Aronian vs. GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov has been one of the big duels in chess for decades, but while age brings experience it also has drawbacks. Aronian won the blitz but lost the rapid and then commented, "I just got way too tired," to mount a comeback in the classical game.

Mamedyarov and Aronian met again. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

In the other clash, meanwhile, GM Wesley So, rather than continuing his earlier criticism of the tournament, was surprisingly revitalized. He said, "the rest day really helped everybody," thanked his chess colleagues for supporting him, and said "we're getting to the exciting format!"

Wesley So was in great spirits at the start of the knockout. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

The players traded wins in the blitz and drew both rapid games, so that this was the one classical game where both players could afford to make a draw. That also looked the likely outcome, but at the end So took over, with GM Vincent Keymer missing a remarkable chance to escape.

Knockout 5: Carlsen Wins Then Forfeits; Artemiev Dominates Vs. Hong

When Carlsen was asked how his day was going, he responded briefly, "I’m in a little bit of the wrong bracket—otherwise, it’s fine!"

I'm in a little bit of the wrong bracket.

—Magnus Carlsen

Carlsen had ended up in the battle for 17th place after a winless 10 fast-classic games, and the first blitz game could easily have continued that sequence. Carlsen gave up his queen but followed up badly until he was completely busted, but Assaubayeva couldn't quite hold things together at blitz pace.

The first game ultimately set the tone for the match. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

That win opened the floodgates, as Carlsen went on to score 3.5/4 in blitz, and 8/8 in rapid. With a score of 11.5/12, he was the one player who had wrapped up victory for the day before the classical game.

He had nothing to play for in Total Chess terms, but curiously, his game against Assaubayeva arguably had the highest stakes and was the most anticipated of the day. A draw, and Carlsen would drop below 2800 for the first time in 17 years, while a loss would put him just 0.7 points abo

additionalSources.title: Giri and Firouzja take first-day leads in Total Chess Semifinals
additionalSources.summary: The knockout stage brought Blitz, Rapid and Fast Classic together on the same day for the first time, with all 24 players back in action across six brackets Anish Giri and Alireza Firouzja won the first day of their semifinals as the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot moved into the knockout stage in Budapest on Tuesday. Giri beat top seed Maxime Vachier-Lagrave by 14.5 points to 5.5, while Firouzja took the day against Fabiano Caruana by 12 points to 8. The four group winners came through five days of Fast Classic to reach the title bracket. Vachier-Lagrave and Caruana were the top scorers of the group stage with 17 points each, winning Groups D and B, while Firouzja took Group A and Giri won Group C on 15 points. The opening-night blitz then set the pairings: Vachier-Lagrave’s second place in the Blitz Swiss made him top seed and set up a meeting with Giri, while Firouzja and Caruana met in the other semifinal. Each knockout day includes seven games: four blitz at 3+2, two rapid at 15+10 and one Fast Classic at 45+30. A blitz win is worth one point, a rapid win four and a Fast Classic win eight, with half for a draw, so a single Fast Classic win outweighs a clean sweep of the blitz. The score resets overnight and Wednesday starts from zero. Wednesday brings the same pairings again, and the second day is decisive: the two match winners go through to the final on Thursday and Friday, while the losers drop out of the title race and into the match for third place. That leaves Giri and Firouzja one drawn day away from the final. Vachier-Lagrave and Caruana must win on Wednesday to force an Armageddon game at the end of the day, where the player with more points over the two days chooses colour. Giri’s Fast Classic win settles the day against Vachier-Lagrave Giri narrowly won the blitz segment 2.5-1.5 against Vachier-Lagrave, and both rapid games were drawn, so Giri took a one-point lead, 6.5-5.5, heading into the Fast Classic game. He then won it with the white pieces, worth eight points, to take the day 14.5-5.5 against the top seed. Firouzja answers Caruana’s fightback Firouzja swept all four blitz games against Caruana, the joint top scorer of the group stage, to open with a 4-0 lead. Caruana hit back immediately, winning the first rapid game with the black pieces to level the day at 4-4, but Firouzja responded in kind with a black win of his own in the second rapid game and led 8-4 going into the Fast Classic game. A draw there was enough to give him the day 12-8. Every player still in action Magnus Carlsen, who won the opening Blitz Swiss but went through the group stage without a Fast Classic win, faced Bibisara Assaubayeva in the bracket for places 17 to 20. Back in the faster formats, he took the four blitz games 3.5-0.5 and won both rapid games. Having already clinched the day’s match 11.5-0.5, Carlsen forfeited his Fast Classic game. The biggest turnaround of the day came in the bracket for places 9 to 12, where Haik Martirosyan trailed home favourite Richard Rapport 3-9 going into the Fast Classic game, then won it with the black pieces to take the day 11-9. Hans Moke Niemann and Wesley So also used the eight-point game to turn their days around, Niemann beating Le Quang Liem 13.5-6.5 and So defeating Vincent Keymer 14-6. Day one in the other brackets: Places 5 to 8: Hans Moke Niemann 13.5-6.5 Le QuangLiem; Ian Nepomniachtchi 15-5 Jan-Krzysztof Duda Places 9 to 12: Arjun Erigaisi 11.5-8.5 Jorden van Foreest; Richard Rapport 9-11 Haik Martirosyan Places 13 to 16: Levon Aronian 9-11 Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, Vincent Keymer 6-14 Wesley So Places 17 to 20: Magnus Carlsen 11.5-8.5 Bibisara Assaubayeva, Vladislav Artemiev 17-3 Andrew Hong Places 21 to 24: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu 11-9 Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Vaishali Rameshbabu 7-13 Abhimanyu Mishra Among the Indian players, Arjun Erigaisi won his first day against Jorden van Foreest 11.5-8.5 in the bracket for places 9 to 12. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu recovered from a 1-3 deficit after the blitz, winning the first rapid game and holding the Fast Classic to beat Nodirbek Abdusattorov 11-9 in the bracket for places 21 to 24.  Vaishali Rameshbabu held Abhimanyu Mishra to a draw in the last Fast Classic game of the day to finish, but Mishra’s lead from the blitz and rapid gave him the day 13-7. Complete results: totalchess.com/tournaments/budapest-2026 The semifinals conclude on Wednesday 18 November with the same order of play: blitz from 15:00 CET, rapid at 16:15 and 17:30 and the Fast Classic game at 18:45, followed by Armageddon where needed. The finals and third-place matches in all six brackets are played on 19 and 20 November, when the winner of the first Total Chess event is decided. A total of $650,000 in prize money is at stake across the six brackets. Tuesday was the first time the full Total Chess format, with Blitz, Rapid and Fast Classic counting in the same match, was played in competition. Testing the format in a live competitive environment is one of the primary objectives of the Budapest pilot, together with seeing how the rules work in practice and evaluating whether certain aspects of the regulations could be refined. The format and regulations were developed with considerable thought and input, but the real test is how they work in live competition. Total Chess will gather feedback from players, arbiters and other stakeholders and assess whether any refinements are needed before the inaugural season begins in March 2027. There is no predetermined view that the rules need to change; the aim is to test the format thoroughly and take the best possible version of it into the first full season. Text: Total Chess Photos: Maria Emelianova and Michal Walusza Official website: www.totalchess.com About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive

title: Gukesh Opens Up About Pressure, Criticism Ahead Of Sindarov Match
summary:
World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju says he has struggled to handle the pressure and expectations of the world title, and is finding ways to deal with the criticism ahead of his match against GM Javokhir Sindarov.

“I think clearly so far I've not been able to handle it in the best possible way,” he said.

Gukesh was speaking during a dinner conversation with five-time world champion GM Viswanathan Anand and ChessBase India co-founder IM Sagar Shah, filmed at Anand's home in Chennai. The video was released by Chess.com last week.

You can watch the entire video below.

The entertaining 86-minute conversation ranged from handling criticism and preparing for the world championship to food, encounters with fans, and memories of their early meetings. Alongside many jokes, the two world champions offered reflections on ambition, setbacks, and life outside of chess.

The reigning world champion has had a difficult year, dropping to 28th in the world with a 2710 rating after a string of poor results. He scored 3.5/9 in the Prague Masters in March, and 3/10 in Norway Chess in June before his slump continued with 2/7 in July's Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters, costing him another 14 rating points. He finished last or tied for last in all three events.

His 8.5/11 for India at the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad offered some encouragement, helping his team win the silver medal. However, the 20-year-old still needs to rediscover the form that carried him all the way to the world title in 2024.

When the conversation turned to his recent results, Gukesh was quick to acknowledge how badly things had gone. “There have been maybe two or three tournaments in the last one year that I've been happy about,” he said. “There have been major setbacks.”

Gukesh pointed to missed opportunities in Chennai, and said he had failed to convert positions he felt he would normally win. He believed the difficulties went beyond weaknesses in his chess.

“Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure that I'm dealing with and I've not found the right way to maybe handle it,” he said.

Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure, that I'm dealing with and I've not found the right way to maybe handle it.

—Gukesh Dommaraju

Gukesh during Norway Chess 2026, which ended in another setback for the world champion. Photo: Michal Walusza/Norway Chess.

The world champion said that his approach to dealing with the pressure involves finding more enjoyment in everyday life.

"I'm trying to be happy every day, smile every day," he said. "I'm working hard, but I'm also trying to make sure that I do things that I enjoy outside of chess."

From being a student to being a bro ft. Gukesh! @vishy64theking @DGukesh https://t.co/uUEELo85pR

— Chess.com - India (@chesscom_in) November 16, 2026

Anand, who has experienced difficult periods during his long career, was supportive of that approach.

“I think the day you start to come back is when you stop expecting things. You just try to play a good game of chess,” Anand said. “Take it one step at a time and stop trying to come back to something.”

I think the day you start to come back is when you stop expecting things.

—Viswanathan Anand

Vishy Anand (@vishy64theking) teases Gukesh! https://t.co/lnFaPuHkfT

— Chess.com - India (@chesscom_in) November 14, 2026

Anand explained that the best performances tend to come when a player can return to a natural state, concentrating on the moves rather than carrying their own expectations and those of everyone watching. He described Gukesh’s effort to get a smile back on his face as "basically the correct attitude."

The conversation also touched on the criticism that accompanies the world title. "For a long time I was trying to avoid criticism," he said. "Even if you're trying to avoid, you know that people are saying things."

A friend had suggested drawing on his enjoyment of comedy to respond with humor instead. "I like humor. I like comedy," Gukesh explained, recalling the suggestion: "When you come across some hater, why don't you just play along with them?”

Gukesh scored 8.5/11 as India won silver at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

Anand agreed that public expectations can reach a player despite their best efforts to concentrate on chess. “Somewhere deep down you can't push the thought completely away,” he said.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world champion at 18 by defeating GM Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024. His first title defense will begin with the opening game in Geneva on November 24, against a challenger who won both the 2025 World Cup and the 2026 Candidates Tournament.

Sindarov's results present a sharp contrast to Gukesh. He has a 2812 rating performance in the last 12 months, the highest in the world. Gukesh, on the other hand, is 39th on the same list with 2654.

Despite his struggles, Gukesh believes his match experience can help him against Sindarov. "It's about who manages to stay in good shape and is able to handle and absorb the pressure and deliver when the day comes," he said. "I do have more experience than him. I've played a world championship."

It's about who manages to stay in good shape and is able to handle and absorb the pressure and deliver when the day comes.

—Gukesh Dommaraju

Gukesh also noted that his Singapore match went down to the final classical game. He already knows how the tension builds, how much energy preparation consumes, and how difficult it can be simply to return to the board each day.

"Every day you're going to wake up with like butterflies in your stomach," he said.

Anand warned that championship pressure can push players beyond their usual limits in either direction, producing exceptional chess as well as mistakes they might not otherwise make.

"In a world championship, the players will do things that they won't normally do," he said. "You should be ready for very unexpected things to happen."

In a world championship, the players will do things that they won't normally do. You should be ready for very unexpected things to happen.

—Viswanathan Anand

The Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 kicks off in Geneva at 15:00 CET on Tuesday, November 24!
